question_text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of recurrent nosebleeds and fatigue for the past 2 months. He also frequently complains his head hurts. The patient has met all motoric milestones for his age but does not like to run because his legs start to hurt if he does. He is at the 40th percentile for both height and weight. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard in the left paravertebral region. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Question
                    A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of recurrent nosebleeds and fatigue for the past 2 months. He also frequently complains his head hurts. The patient has met all motoric milestones for his age but does not like to run because his legs start to hurt if he does. He is at the 40th percentile for both height and weight. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure in the right arm is 130/85 mm Hg. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard in the left paravertebral region. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Inferior rib notching
opb. Interarm difference in tissue oxygenation
opc. Pulmonary valve stenosis
opd. Left-axis deviation on ECG
ope. Delayed pulse in lower extremities

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent nosebleeds, fatigue, headaches, and leg pain during running, alongside elevated blood pressure (130/85 mm Hg) and a systolic murmur in the left paravertebral region. These findings suggest a possible coarctation of the aorta, which is known to cause systemic hypertension and can lead to inferior rib notching due to collateral circulation. The presence of leg pain during exertion and elevated blood pressure supports this diagnosis, as coarctation can result in delayed pulses in the lower extremities. While left-axis deviation on ECG may occur due to left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension, it is not definitive without further testing. Pulmonary valve stenosis is unlikely as it does not typically correlate with the symptoms presented. Therefore, the most likely finding upon further evaluation is inferior rib notching, which is a classic sign of aortic coarctation.
